samples.summary: ReDoS in `SAFE_COLOR_RE`: peer-controlled presence `color` reaches an ambiguous nested-quantifier regex bounded only at 64 chars, enough for ~10^9 backtracks and a frozen editor on every other client
samples.evidence: `sanitizePeerColor` (remote-selection.ts:80-87) accepts any string up to 64 chars and tests it against `SAFE_COLOR_RE` (:58), whose function branch is `(?:rgb|rgba|hsl|hsla)\((?:\s*[-+]?[0-9]*\.?[0-9]+(?:%|deg|...)?\s*[,/]?\s*){3,4}\)`. The inner `[0-9]*\.?[0-9]+` is ambiguous (for a digit run of length k there are ~k ways to split it), and the group repeats 3-4 times, so a non-matching input explores ~sum over compositions of the digit budget of the product of part lengths. Attack: a client that can attach to the note document (any collaborator, or a share-link visitor via `shared-document.tsx:887` presence) sets `presence.color = 'hsl(' + '1'.repeat(60)` — 64 chars, so the length guard at :85 passes and there is no ')' so the match must fail. Generating function x^4/(1-x)^8 gives ~C(64,8) ≈ 4.4e9 backtracking paths for the 4-iteration branch alone. `sanitizePeerColor` is called once per peer inside `buildDecorations` (:170), which runs on *every* ViewUpdate and on every presence event (:140-142), so the main thread of every other viewer's tab stalls indefinitely — a persistent client-side DoS delivered through unvalidated presence data. The 64-char cap the comment at :83-85 relies on is only adequate for a linear pattern; for this degree-~8 blowup it is not a bound. Fix: make each argument unambiguous (`[0-9]+(?:\.[0-9]+)?`) and/or drop the cap to ~24. The new test at remote-selection.test.ts:130-141 only feeds `'x'.repeat(200)`, which is rejected by the length check before the regex runs, so the suite is green with the hole open.

samples.summary: `sanitizeDisplayName` runs two global Unicode regex passes over the entire untrusted string before capping length, so a huge self-reported name/attribute costs O(size) on every keystroke for every viewer
samples.evidence: `sanitizeDisplayName` does `.replace(INVISIBLE_RE,'').replace(UNICODE_SPACE_RE,' ').slice(0,64)` — the two `u`-flagged global scans happen on the *full* attacker-supplied value, and only then is it truncated. The value is unvalidated peer data on both paths: `remote-selection.ts:219` calls it once per peer inside `buildDecorations`, which reruns on every ViewUpdate/presence event, and `blame-gutter.ts:56` plus `yorkie-note-store.ts:222` call it once per CRDT run on every doc change. A malicious client that sets a multi-megabyte `presence.name`, or writes a multi-megabyte `a` attribute on many runs directly against Yorkie (nothing validates change contents — see the trust-boundary note at yorkie-note-store.ts:19-45), makes every other client scan megabytes per keystroke, i.e. an unusable editor. Cheap fix: `value.slice(0, MAX_DISPLAY_NAME_LENGTH * 4)` before the regex passes. Confidence is low only because I could not confirm how large a presence payload / run attribute the Yorkie server will relay.

samples.summary: The `t` clamp within the skew window still lets a forged run outrank every genuine edit on its line, contradicting the "at most a tie that document order breaks" claim the control is documented with
samples.evidence: `sanitizeWrittenAt` discards `t > now + 5min` but otherwise returns `Math.min(value, now)` (yorkie-note-store.ts:96). A client writing `t = Date.now() + 299_000` therefore reads back as `at === now` on every recompute for the next ~5 minutes, and afterwards as a fixed timestamp still later than every edit made before it. `authorOfRange` (packages/notes/src/view/blame-gutter.ts:49) picks the span with the greatest `at`, so the forged run wins the line outright — not "a tie that document order breaks", as the comment at yorkie-note-store.ts:80-88 and docs/design/notes/notes.md:597-604 state. A hostile client can also re-stamp the attribute periodically to keep the window fresh. Impact is bounded to label spoofing (the gutter is explicitly not an audit trail), but the mitigation is weaker than its own documentation claims, which is how a weak control gets relied on later.

samples.summary: Durable identity disclosure is gated on a single global, cross-note preference whose warning appears only in a hover `title`, and a recorded name can never be redacted
samples.evidence: `readShowAuthors`/`writeShowAuthors` persist one global key `wafflebase:notes:showAuthors` (notes-settings.ts:11), which `notes-detail.tsx:47` feeds to both the gutter and `YorkieNoteStore({ recordAuthorship })` (notes-view.tsx:121). Consequence: a user who enables the gutter once — perhaps on a private note to read history — thereafter writes `{ a: <username> }` into the content of *every* note they edit (yorkie-note-store.ts:187-193), including notes owned by others and notes exposed through viewer-role share links (`shared-document.tsx:883-897` renders notes to anonymous visitors), where the username becomes readable by anyone holding the link and by anyone who reads the note later. The only disclosure notice is a `title` tooltip on the dropdown item (notes-toolbar.tsx:370) — invisible on touch and to keyboard users, and never shown again while recording continues. Because the CRDT is append-only, there is no path to redact a name once written (docs/design/notes/notes.md notes retention is deliberately unbounded). Scoping the recording half per document, or surfacing an on-screen indicator while it is active, would match the consent to the exposure.

samples.summary: `sanitizeDisplayName` truncates after stripping lone surrogates and does not bound combining marks, so the cap can reintroduce an unpaired surrogate and a Zalgo name can still paint outside its label
samples.evidence: `\p{Cs}` is stripped at line 53 but `.slice(0, 64)` at line 55 runs afterwards on UTF-16 code units, so cutting an astral character in half puts an unpaired surrogate back into the value that becomes DOM (`blame-gutter.ts:112`/`118`, `remote-selection.ts:106`). Separately, no combining-mark limit is applied: 64 stacked U+0300s in a self-reported name render far outside `.cm-ySelectionInfo`, which has `position:absolute; whiteSpace:nowrap; zIndex:101` and no overflow clipping (remote-selection.ts:28-44), letting a peer paint over the document text of everyone else. Both are UI-spoofing hardening on a path this change explicitly hardens elsewhere; grapheme-aware truncation plus a per-base combining-mark cap would close them.

samples.summary: Nothing bounds the size of an incoming `a`/`t` run attribute, so a hostile client can permanently bloat a note's CRDT with attribute payloads the read path merely truncates for display
samples.evidence: The write path caps its own name (`sanitizeDisplayName(...) ?? ''`, yorkie-note-store.ts:191), but the read path only sanitizes for display (:222) — the underlying attribute stays whatever a client sent. Since Yorkie validates nothing inside a change and the backend never inspects note content (the auth webhook authorizes docKey+verb only, per the note at :19-45), any client with write access can attach megabyte-scale `a` attributes to many runs; the data is permanent (append-only history), inflates every future snapshot/attach for all readers, and is invisible in the rendered text so it will not be noticed. Searched for any size/shape validation of note changes: grepped `getAuthorSpans`, `AUTHOR_ATTR`, `content.edit(` across the repo and the backend webhook path referenced in the file header; found none. Storage-abuse hardening rather than an immediate exploit, hence minor.

verdict.reason: Verified in-repo. SAFE_COLOR_RE (remote-selection.ts:57-58) contains the ambiguous nested quantifier `[0-9]*\.?[0-9]+` inside a `{3,4}` group; sanitizePeerColor (:80-87) admits any string up to 64 chars into `.test()`. For a non-matching input such as 'hsl(' + '1'.repeat(60) (64 chars, passes the cap at :85, no closing paren so the match must fail), the backtracking engine enumerates ~C(64,8) ~ 4.4e9 split assignments (generating function x^4/(1-x)^8 summed over prefixes); V8's Irregexp does not memoize, so this is a multi-second-to-minutes main-thread stall. The value is genuinely attacker-controlled and unguarded: yorkie-note-store.ts:475 copies raw `peer.presence.color` into NotePeerSelection, and remote-selection.ts:170 sanitizes it per peer inside buildDecorations, which runs on construction (:139), on every ViewUpdate (:160), and on every presence event (:140-142). No upstream validation exists (MemNoteStore never emits presence, memory.ts:216), and the new test only feeds 'x'.repeat(200) (remote-selection.test.ts:134), which the length check rejects before the regex runs. In-lane as untrusted-input handling / ReDoS with a real client-side DoS impact.

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as the reviewer describes. display-name.ts:52-56 runs two global `u`-flagged regex passes (INVISIBLE_RE at :31-32, UNICODE_SPACE_RE at :38) over the entire untrusted string and only truncates afterwards at :55. All three call sites are real and reachable with attacker-controlled data: remote-selection.ts:219 (per peer, per decoration rebuild), blame-gutter.ts:56 inside authorOfRange, which computeBlameLabels calls once per document line (:71-79) and NoteBlameTracker.update reruns on every docChanged (:145-154), and yorkie-note-store.ts:222 once per CRDT run. The repository's own trust-boundary note at yorkie-note-store.ts:21-46 states Yorkie validates nothing inside a change and a client can claim any name on any run, so the values are genuinely unvalidated peer input. I grepped for any upstream length bound on presence names or the `a` attribute and found none — the only cap is MAX_DISPLAY_NAME_LENGTH, applied after the scans — so `already-guarded` does not apply and `not-present` is disproven. I considered `out-of-scope` (availability rather than authz/secrets/injection/crypto), but the lens's exclusion list does not cover untrusted-input resource exhaustion, and the per-line rescan yields genuine amplification (attacker pays N once; each victim pays lines x N per keystroke), which exceeds the baseline cost a collaborator could already impose by writing large text. Remaining uncertainty is only the server-relayed payload ceiling, which bounds magnitude, not existence.

finding.summary: Peer-controlled `color` is interpolated raw into a `style` attribute (CSS injection), in the same function the diff hardens for `name`
finding.evidence: The diff sanitizes the self-reported presence `name` at remote-selection.ts:175 (`sanitizeDisplayName(peer.name)`) and states that both render paths now "share one guarantee" for unverified presence data. The sibling untrusted presence field on the very same object is still interpolated verbatim into an attribute string: `attributes: { style: `background-color: ${peer.color}` }` (remote-selection.ts:146). `peer.color` comes from `NotesPresence.color` (packages/frontend/src/types/notes-document.ts:35), a free-form string each client sets for itself; the backend never validates presence (yorkie-auth.controller.ts authorizes docKey+verb only) and Yorkie validates nothing inside a change. Vector: a co-editor (or an anonymous share-link editor, role `editor` per yorkie-auth.controller.ts:200) attaches with `color: "red; position:fixed; inset:0; width:100vw; height:100vh; z-index:99999; background-image:url(https://attacker/beacon)"`. CodeMirror passes the attribute map to `setAttribute('style', ...)`, so every declaration applies on every other viewer's screen: full-viewport overlay (UI spoofing / clickjacking over the editor) plus an outbound request that discloses each viewer's IP/UA to the attacker. Not XSS (attribute, not HTML), but arbitrary attacker CSS in another user's document view. Only occurrence of this template in the repo (grep `background-color: \$\{`). The line predates the diff, but the diff is exactly the change that audits this data flow and it stops one field short; `peer.color` is also used safely two lines away via `span.style.backgroundColor = this.color` (line 61), which shows the safe form.

verdict.reason: The finding claims `peer.color` is interpolated verbatim into a style attribute at remote-selection.ts:146. That code is not present. The sole occurrence of the `background-color: ${...}` template in the source tree is remote-selection.ts:189, and it interpolates the local `color`, which is produced at remote-selection.ts:170 by `sanitizePeerColor(peer.color)`. `sanitizePeerColor` (lines 80-87) is a recognize-or-replace validator: non-strings, empty values, and values over 64 chars return `FALLBACK_PEER_COLOR` (#9ca3af, line 61), and the anchored SAFE_COLOR_RE (line 57-58) admits only `#hex`, a bare `[a-z]{3,20}` keyword, or `rgb/rgba/hsl/hsla()` with numeric/percent/angle arguments — no alternative can contain `;`, `}`, a quote, or `url(`, so the exact payload in the finding's vector is rejected before reaching CodeMirror's attribute map. A grep of `packages/notes/src` shows line 170 is the only read of `peer.color`; the caret widget at lines 217-220 receives the already-sanitized `color`, so both DOM routes are covered. The quoted string `style: \`background-color: ${peer.color}\`` exists in the repo only in an archived task document (docs/tasks/archive/2026/07/20260715-notes-markdown-type-todo.md:852), i.e. a historical snapshot, not executable code. The finding's core premise — that the hardening pass covered `name` but stopped short of `color` — is contradicted by lines 167-170 and 217-220, which sanitize both.

finding.summary: Editor usernames are now permanently persisted into note content and disclosed to every reader (incl. viewer-role share links), with recording unconditional and no opt-out
finding.evidence: `editText` unconditionally stamps `{ a: <presence name>, t: Date.now() }` on every inserted run (yorkie-note-store.ts:145-151). The presence `name` is the authenticated user's username (notes-detail.tsx:259 `name: currentUser.username`). The `showAuthors` preference added by this change is display-only and per-reader (notes-settings.ts / notes-view.tsx): a user who never enables the gutter still has their username written into the CRDT on every keystroke, and there is no setting that stops recording. Because the attributes live inside `root.content`, they are part of the document snapshot delivered to ANY principal with read access — including an anonymous viewer-role share-link visitor, who is granted read by yorkie-auth.controller.ts:200 (`return needWrite ? link.role === 'editor' : true`) and whose UI (SharedNotesLayout, shared-document.tsx:322-348) never surfaces the gutter but whose client still receives the attributes and can dump them from the console. Before this change a share visitor learned only the identities of users concurrently connected (ephemeral presence); afterwards they learn the username of every past editor of every line, retained indefinitely (docs/design/notes/notes.md: "Retention ... is deliberately unbounded for now"). Confidence is low because presence already leaks username/email of online users to share visitors, so the delta is historical/offline members rather than a wholly new class of data.

verdict.reason: The finding's factual premise is not present in this repository. Authorship recording is NOT unconditional: `editText` writes the `{a, t}` attributes only under `if (insert.length > 0 && this.recordAuthorship)` (yorkie-note-store.ts:186), falling through to an unattributed `root.content.edit(from, to, insert)` otherwise (yorkie-note-store.ts:195). It defaults to OFF (`options.recordAuthorship ?? false`, yorkie-note-store.ts:149; `showAuthors = false` default at notes-view.tsx:88; `readShowAuthors()` only true for an explicit stored "true", notes-settings.ts:46-48). The `showAuthors` preference is NOT display-only: the sole production caller wires it into the store at notes-view.tsx:121 (`new YorkieNoteStore(doc, { recordAuthorship: showAuthors })`) and keeps it in sync live at notes-view.tsx:166-169 (`storeRef.current?.setRecordAuthorship(showAuthors)`), so an opt-out stops recording on the next keystroke (`setRecordAuthorship`, yorkie-note-store.ts:174-176). A grep over packages/** for `recordAuthorship` found no other production call site passing true. The reviewer's cited line range 145-151 is the constructor, not `editText`. What remains is the deliberate, explicitly opt-in disclosure of the user's own presence display name — a name already broadcast to the same readers via peer-caret presence — documented at yorkie-note-store.ts:48-64; that is not a missing/bypassable authorization gate, secret exposure, or injection under the security rubric.

finding.summary: Blame attribution is derived entirely from client-controlled presence with no server-side verification, so any editor can forge another user's authorship
finding.evidence: `localAuthorName()` reads `this.doc.getMyPresence()?.name` (yorkie-note-store.ts:135) — a value the client itself set at attach time (notes-detail.tsx:259, shared-document.tsx:890). Presence content is never validated: I found no server-side check of presence or of `Text` attributes (yorkie-auth.controller.ts only authorizes doc key + verb; yorkie-event.controller.ts has no username/identity handling; note-content.ts ignores attributes). A malicious client with write access — including an *anonymous* share-link visitor, since yorkie-auth.controller.ts:200 grants `rw` to `link.role === 'editor'` with no login — can call `presence.set({ name: 'victim-username' })`, or write the attributes directly as `content.edit(from, to, text, { a: 'victim-username', t: Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER })`. Because `authorOfRange` picks the run with the largest `at` (blame-gutter.ts:48) and `t` is a client-supplied `Date.now()`, a forged far-future timestamp lets an attacker permanently own the displayed author of any line they touch by one character — e.g. insert a space into a victim's line, or attribute their own defamatory text to the victim. The gutter presents this as fact ("who last edited each line", editor.ts:122) with no trust indicator; homoglyph/RTL-override or zero-width names sharpen the impersonation (`author.trim() === ''` only catches pure whitespace, blame-gutter.ts:51). Mitigating: docs/design/notes/notes.md explicitly calls blame "a reading aid, not an audit trail" — but that caveat is not surfaced in the UI. Amplifier, pre-existing and out of diff: the auth webhook runs in shadow mode unless `YORKIE_AUTH_WEBHOOK_ENFORCE === 'true'` (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:86-105), so today even the editor-role gate is not enforced.

verdict.reason: Every control the finding says is missing exists in the repo. (1) The claimed exploit "a forged far-future t permanently owns the line" is defeated by sanitizeWrittenAt (yorkie-note-store.ts:91-97), which DISCARDS any t > now+5min as 0 (below every real edit) rather than clamping — applied on every read at :223 and covered by tests (yorkie-note-store.test.ts:233-264). (2) The quoted evidence line `author.trim() === ''` at blame-gutter.ts:51 does not exist; blame-gutter.ts:56 calls sanitizeDisplayName, and display-name.ts:31-56 strips C0/C1 controls, Cf/bidi overrides, zero-width, surrogates, private-use and invisible non-Cf code points, folds Unicode spaces, and caps at 64 chars — applied on write (yorkie-note-store.ts:191), on read (:222), and again at the DOM boundary (tests at yorkie-note-store.test.ts:280-297). (3) The claim "gutter presents this as fact with no trust indicator / the caveat is not surfaced in the UI" is directly contradicted by blame-gutter.ts:118, which renders the hover title as "<name> (self-reported)". (4) I enumerated all consumers of getAuthorSpans(): only blame-gutter.ts:138,149 plus tests — no permission, audit, or backend path reads it, so the value is never an authorization input. The residual (no server-signed provenance) is real, explicitly documented as a deliberate trust boundary (yorkie-note-store.ts:21-46, docs/design/notes/notes.md:582-628), display-only, and bounded by the guards above — a hardening item, not a blocking auth/crypto/injection defect under this lens.
